'''''Bauhinia purpurea''''' is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Fabaceae]], native to the [[Indian subcontinent]] and [[Myanmar]], and widely introduced elsewhere in tropical and subtropical areas of the world. Common names include '''orchid tree''',<ref name="GRIN">{{Cite web |title=Bauhinia purpurea L.  GRIN-Global |url=https://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxon/taxonomydetail?id=6590 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250414014354/https://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxon/taxonomydetail?id=6590 |archive-date=2025-04-14 |access-date=2025-12-04 |website=npgsweb.ars-grin.gov |language=en}}</ref> '''purple bauhinia''',<ref name=GRIN/> '''camel's foot''',<ref name=GRIN/> '''butterfly tree''',<ref name=GRIN/> and '''Hawaiian orchid tree'''.{{cn|date=December 2025}}

==Description==
''Bauhinia purpurea'' is a small to medium-size [[deciduous]] tree growing to {{convert|17|ft|order=flip}} tall. The [[leaves]] are alternate, {{convert|10|–|20|cm|frac=2}} long and broad, rounded, and bilobed at the base and apex. The [[flower]]s are conspicuous, pink, and fragrant, with five petals. The [[fruit]] is a [[legume|pod]] measuring {{convert|30|cm|abbr=on|frac=2}} long, containing 12 to 16 [[seed]]s. As a diploid species with 28 chromosomes, sequencing of the 304MB ''B. purpurea'' genome was used to demonstrate it is the maternal ancestor of the hybrid [[Bauhinia × blakeana|Hong Kong Bauhinia (''Bauhinia x blakeana'')]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mu |first1=Weixue |last2=Darian |first2=Joshua Casey |last3=Sung |first3=Wing-Kin |last4=Guo |first4=Xing |last5=Yang |first5=Tuo |last6=Tang |first6=Mandy Wai Man |last7=Chen |first7=Ziqiang |last8=Tong |first8=Steve Kwan Hok |last9=Chik |first9=Irene Wing Shan |last10=Davidson |first10=Robert L |last11=Edmunds |first11=Scott C |last12=Wei |first12=Tong |last13=Tsui |first13=Stephen Kwok-Wing |date=2025-01-01 |title=The haplotype-resolved T2T genome for Bauhinia × blakeana sheds light on the genetic basis of flower heterosis |url=https://doi.org/10.1093/gigascience/giaf044 |journal=GigaScience |volume=14 |article-number=giaf044 |doi=10.1093/gigascience/giaf044 |issn=2047-217X |pmc=12012898 |pmid=40276955}}</ref> 

=== Chemistry ===
A wide range of chemical compounds have been isolated from ''Bauhinia purpurea'' including 5,6-dihydroxy-7-methoxyflavone 6-''O''-β-<small>D</small>-xylopyranoside, bis [3',4'-dihydroxy-6-methoxy-7,8-furano-5',6'-mono-methylalloxy]-5-''C''-5-biflavonyl and (4'-hydroxy-7-methyl 3-''C''-α-<small>L</small>-rhamnopyranosyl)-5-''C''-5-(4'-hydroxy-7-methyl-3-''C''-α-<small>D</small>-glucopyranosyl) bioflavonoid, [[Dihydrostilbenoid|bibenzyl]]s, [[dibenzoxepin]]s, mixture of [[phytol]] fatty esters, [[lutein]], [[β-sitosterol]], [[isoquercitin]] and [[astragalin]].{{Citation needed|date=December 2019|reason=removed citation to predatory publisher}}

==Distribution and habitat==
Native to the [[Indian subcontinent]] and [[Myanmar]], the species has been widely introduced elsewhere in tropical and subtropical areas of the world.<ref name="POWO_481605-1" /> 

In the United States, the tree grows in [[Hawaii]], coastal [[California]], southern [[Texas]], and southwest [[Florida]]. [[Bauhinia × blakeana|''Bauhinia'' × ''blakeana'']] is usually propagated by [[grafting]] it onto ''B. purpurea'' stems.{{Citation needed|date=September 2024}}

==Uses==
The young leaves and flowers of ''Bauhinia purpurea'' are edible.<ref name="wac"/> In the [[Philippines]], ''B. purpurea'' is known as ''alibangbang''<ref>{{cite book  |url=https://quod.lib.umich.edu/p/philamer/AGJ6434.0001.001/130 |via=University of Michigan Digital Collections |title=A dictionary of the plant names of the Philippine Islands |first1=Elmer Drew |last1=Merrill |page=128 |publisher=Bureau of Public Printing, [[Department of the Interior and Local Government|Department of The Interior]] |location= Manila  |date=1903 }}</ref> (lit. "butterfly"). The leaves have a citrusy and sour taste and are used either as a souring agent for ''[[sinigang]]'' and similar dishes, or, as a pickle condiment, in [[Philippine cuisine]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Alibangbang / Malabar Bauhinia |url=http://www.marketmanila.com/archives/alibangbang-malabar-bauhinia |website=Market Manila |date=7 August 2006 |accessdate=26 November 2019}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Vanzi |first1=Sol |title=Sinigang secrets: Sinigang is life |url=https://lifestyle.mb.com.ph/2017/08/17/sinigang-secrets/ |accessdate=26 November 2019 |work=Manila Bulletin |date=17 August 2017 |archive-date=6 June 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190606170358/https://lifestyle.mb.com.ph/2017/08/17/sinigang-secrets/ |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Seidemann |first1=Johannes |title=World Spice Plants |date=2005 |publisher=Springer-Verlag Berlin Heidelberg |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |isbn=9783540279082 |page=64}}</ref>

Throughout [[Southeast Asia]], ''B. purpurea'' and related species are also used in making poultices for treating swelling, bruises, boils, and ulcers. Various parts of the plant are also used in decoctions to treat fever and stomach ailments, as well as being used as an [[astringent]].<ref name="wac">{{cite web |title=''Bauhinia purpurea'' |url=http://old.worldagroforestry.org/treedb/AFTPDFS/Bauhinia_purpurea.PDF |website=Agroforestree database |publisher=World Agroforestry Centre |accessdate=26 November 2019}}</ref> 

In Indian traditional medicine, the leaves are used to treat coughs while the bark is used for glandular diseases and as an antidote for poisons. The flowers are also used in [[South Asian pickles|pickles]] and [[curries]] and is regarded as a [[laxative]].<ref name="wac"/>
